summary: C.E.R. NASA PSI — Habitat Fire Safety Mission Control is an interactive AI-powered web dashboard and 3D tactical simulator designed to summarize, rank, and interpret NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity combustion experiments for spacecraft, lunar bases, and pressurized rovers. Directly addressing the Flame in Freefall challenge, our platform translates decades of complex orbital fire science—spanning facilities like the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), and Cygnus Saffire vehicles—into actionable fire prevention, smoke detection, and suppression protocols. As humanity returns to the Moon under the Artemis program, habitats will operate in reduced gravity (1/6g) and oxygenenriched, hypobaric atmospheres (such as 34% O₂ at 8.2 psi) where fire behaves unpredictably. Our tool bridges critical experimental data gaps and delivers life-saving engineering insights for both space mission planners and terrestrial fire safety applications.
details:
What it does Our project is an AI-powered fire-safety dashboard for human space exploration, built on NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion data. NASA’s microgravity fire research is spread across 24 investigations and thousands of pages of reports, tables and presentations, which makes it hard to find, compare and interpret. Our dashboard puts that knowledge in one place. It lets users explore how fire behaves in different spacecraft and habitat atmospheres, and answers questions using only NASA sources, with a citation on every statement. It has two main sections, Simulation and AI, and works in English and Spanish on desktop and mobile.

How it works 1. Data pipeline (Python) We downloaded 24 PSI combustion investigations: BASS, Saffire, SAME, DAFT, FLEX, CFI, ACME, SLICE, SPICE and related ground studies. We cleaned their experimental tables into one common dataset of 781 tests, each with O₂, pressure, airflow, result and DOI. We extracted the text of their reports, science documents and presentations (PDF, Word, PowerPoint) and split it into 16,353 fragments. Each fragment is turned into a vector with a multilingual embedding model, so a question in Spanish finds documents written in English. Everything is stored in PostgreSQL with pgvector.

2. Scenario simulator Users pick a habitat preset (lunar south-pole base, pressurized rover, EVA airlock, Gateway station) or set their own values: gravity: 0 g, Moon, Mars, Earth, or any value in between O₂ concentration total pressure airflow fuel type: solid, liquid or gas A WebGL flame reacts in real time: in microgravity it becomes the rounder, bluish flame characteristic of the absence of buoyancy. An indicative risk index updates instantly. The dashboard ranks the Top 3 most relevant PSI experiments for that scenario. A 3D viewer shows the Moon, Mars or Earth using NASA imagery, with real sun lighting and the live position of the ISS.

3. AI assistant (retrieval-augmented generation) Search: each question runs a hybrid search that combines meaning (vector similarity) and exact technical keywords (full-text search with a Spanish-to-English glossary). Results are merged and kept diverse across experiments and documents. Answer: the AI receives only the most relevant NASA fragments and must cite each claim with a numbered reference. Each reference opens the experiment’s DOI. Scenario context: the assistant reads the current simulator values. “Interpret this scenario” produces a summary organized by NASA’s three fire-safety pillars: prevention, detection and suppression. Scenario proposals: the AI can suggest scenarios to compare, which the user applies to the simulator with one click and can undo. Automatic checks in code: flags numbers that don’t appear in the sources removes verdicts such as “this scenario is safe” makes sure the safety recommendation always aims to reduce risk blocks harmful requests before they reach the AI

4. ACME test-log analyzer Users open the real log of ACME CLD Flame test day 17319 (Nov 15, 2017): 18 tests that ignited, failed or were aborted. Any test can be loaded into the simulator with one click. For a selected test, the code first builds the verified facts, without AI: what happened, the cause given in the log, the most comparable successful tests, and warnings where the log shows mixed results. The AI then recommends what could have made the test succeed, based only on that log. Any statement that doesn’t match the log is removed automatically.

Benefits Makes NASA data usable: years of microgravity combustion research become searchable and comparable in seconds instead of hours of reading. Trustworthy answers: every claim is traceable to a NASA document and DOI, and the system says so when the data doesn’t cover a question. For example, PSI has no partial-gravity combustion data yet. Safety-first design: the tool supports engineering judgment but does not replace it. It never declares a scenario “safe” and always frames recommendations around reducing fire risk. Accessible: bilingual, mobile-friendly, and adjustable for engineers or students. Learning from failures: the test-log analyzer turns real experiment logs into concrete lessons. What we want to achieve Help mission designers, engineers, researchers, teachers and students understand fire risk in future habitats. Lunar bases are expected to use oxygen-enriched, low-pressure atmospheres, where materials burn more easily. Speed up discovery of the NASA research that matters for new fire-safety equipment.

Next steps: let the AI query the 781-test dataset directly for exact numbers add partial-gravity data as NASA releases it replace simulated parameters with live sensor readings (the dashboard is already designed for this) export filtered data for predictive modeling Tools, languages, hardware and software Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SQL, GLSL (WebGL shaders) Backend: FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, pg8000 Data processing: pypdf, openpyxl, custom parsers for Word and PowerPoint files AI: Groq API running the open-weight model gpt-oss-120b paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 embeddings via fastembed (ONNX Runtime, runs locally) Google Gemini as an optional fallback Database: Supabase (PostgreSQL + pgvector with HNSW index + full-text search) Frontend: Tailwind CSS, three.js, WebGL, Canvas 2D, astronomy-engine (Sun position), satellite.js (ISS orbit from public orbital elements) Data and imagery: NASA PSI repository NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (LRO Moon maps) USGS/NASA/JPL (Viking Mars mosaic) NASA Earth Observatory (Blue Marble, Black Marble) Deployment and collaboration: Git and GitHub, Google Cloud Run with Cloud Build, Cloudflare Tunnel for mobile testing Development assistance: Claude (Anthropic) was used as an AI coding assistant during development. Hardware: no special hardware. It runs in any modern browser, including phones; the server needs about 1 GB of RAM.
